script:
This robot learned to walk on flat ground in under four minutes, and it didn’t even need its real legs.
See all those little guys on the screen?
Those are four thousand virtual copies of a four-legged robot called ANYmal, all running on a single graphics chip.
Think of it like a video game where all the players share one brain.
Each copy tries moving its legs a little differently.
It gets points for walking at the right speed, loses points for banging a knee, and if it lands on its belly, it resets.
So one AI learns from four thousand attempts at the same time.
Even on uneven ground with stairs, training took about twenty minutes.
But here’s the hard part.
A foot that grips the floor in the simulation might slip in the real world.
So the researchers change how slippery the virtual ground is.
They even give these guys a shove every ten seconds so they learn to keep their balance.
Then they load that same AI onto the real robot and test it.
And that’s the wild part. This robot can get better at climbing stairs without changing a thing about its legs.
It just gets a software update.

sources.supports: Four thousand simulated ANYmal quadrupeds train one shared walking policy on a single GPU; speed rewards, knee collision penalties, resets after falling, training times for flat and uneven terrain including stairs, randomized ground friction, virtual pushes every ten seconds, and transfer to the physical robot.
ANYmal learns through trial and error in simulation; improved walking capabilities are tested on physical hardware and deployed as fleet software updates, including improvements in stair climbing.
